title: Intel SGX enclaves
description: SGX carves encrypted memory regions (enclaves) that even the OS and hypervisor can't read; code inside runs with hardware confidentiality and integrity. Remote attestation proves to a verifier what's running inside. The model: trust the CPU, nobody else — enclaves host key managers, private ML, and confidential smart contracts.
method: Partition code into enclave (sensitive) and untrusted (rest); ECALL/OCALL bridge them; attest with IAS/DCAP before provisioning secrets.
usage: Minimize the enclave TCB; attest before provisioning secrets; plan for side-channel hardening.

demo.code:
print('enclave: key_manager (MRENCLAVE a1b2...)')
print('attestation verified -> secrets provisioned into enclave')

title: Intel TDX
description: TDX extends the VM-level confidential computing model to Intel: trust domains are hardware-isolated VMs the hypervisor can't inspect, with attestation via SGX-based quoting. The cloud-native answer for Intel shops — confidential VMs without enclave rewrites.
method: Deploy trust domains; attest via TD quotes; manage like VMs with confidential guarantees.
usage: Use for confidential cloud VMs on Intel; verify quotes in your deployment pipeline.

demo.code:
print('trust domain deployed; TD quote verified')
print('hypervisor sees ciphertext only')

title: Confidential containers
description: Confidential containers (CoCo, Azure ACI) run standard container images inside TEEs — no enclave rewrite needed. The container runtime is measured and attested; the image's layers are verified. It's TEE adoption without the porting tax.
method: Run images under the confidential runtime; attest the runtime + image measurements; standard orchestration outside.
usage: Verify image signatures; attest before scheduling sensitive workloads.

demo.code:
print('pod scheduled on CoCo runtime; image signature + measurement verified')
print('container runs with memory encrypted')

title: Side-channel hardening
description: TEEs don't stop side channels: cache timing, page faults, and speculative execution can leak enclave secrets (Foreshadow, SGX-Step). Hardening means constant-time crypto, disabled hyperthreading where needed, and keeping secrets out of access patterns — the TEE gives confidentiality of data at rest, not of access patterns.
method: Constant-time algorithms; minimize secret-dependent memory access; consider hyperthreading policies; monitor the research.
usage: Threat-model side channels explicitly; constant-time crypto is mandatory, not optional.

demo.code:
print('AES: constant-time implementation (no secret-dependent branches)')
print('access pattern: ORAM for the most sensitive lookups')

title: TEE key management services
description: The canonical TEE workload: keys live and are used inside the enclave — generated there, never exported, operations performed inside. Cloud HSMs and private CAs run this way: the key's entire lifecycle happens behind the hardware boundary.
method: Generate keys in-enclave; expose only operations (sign, decrypt); attest before trusting; log operations outside.
usage: Never export private keys; audit the operation logs; rotate on schedule.

demo.code:
print('CA key generated in-enclave (never exported)')
print('sign(csr) -> certificate; key never left the boundary')

title: Multi-TEE portability
description: SGX, TrustZone, SEV, TDX all differ; portable TEE frameworks (Open Enclave, Veracruz) abstract the differences so one codebase runs across TEEs. Portability avoids hardware lock-in and lets deployments choose the TEE per environment — write once, attest everywhere.
method: Build on a portable framework; abstract attestation verification; test on each target TEE.
usage: Abstract early; verify attestation semantics per TEE (they differ in details).

demo.code:
print('same codebase: SGX in cloud, TrustZone on edge')
print('attestation abstracted; per-TEE verifiers plugged in')

title: Sealing data to enclaves
description: Sealing encrypts data so only the same enclave (same MRENCLAVE, or same signer) can unseal it later — persistent secrets bound to the code identity. Sealed keys survive reboots but not code changes (unless sealed to the signer), tying data to the exact trusted code.
method: Seal with the enclave's seal key; store ciphertext outside; unseal only in the matching enclave; choose MRENCLAVE vs MRSIGNER policy deliberately.
usage: Choose the seal policy for your upgrade story; back up sealed data knowing it binds to code identity.

demo.code:
print('sealed: master_key (policy: MRSIGNER)')
print('upgraded enclave (same signer): unseal OK; different signer: DENIED')

title: Enclave attestation flows
description: Attestation is the TEE's trust handshake: the enclave produces a signed quote of its measurements; the verifier checks the signature chain to the hardware root and compares measurements to known-good values; only then are secrets provisioned. Every TEE integration lives or dies on getting this flow right.
method: Generate quote in-enclave; verify signature chain; compare MRENCLAVE/MRSIGNER to allowlist; provision secrets on success.
usage: Pin the verification logic; allowlist measurements per release; never provision before verification.

demo.code:
print('quote: MRENCLAVE=a1b2, signed by Intel')
print('verify: chain OK, measurement allowlisted -> provision API keys')
